articles.title: Healthcare workers respond to a broken system by unionizing
articles.author: Dennis Kosuth
articles.content: C hicago is seeing a burst of unionization amongst registered nurses – and it has become infectious, in the best sense of that word. In May of 2026, 77 percent of nurses at Rush University Medical Center (RUMC) voted in favor of joining the National Nurses Organizing Committee (NNOC). The 1,700 nurses at RUMC are now part of National Nurses United (NNU), a union that represents 225,000 nurses in healthcare settings across the United States. NNU was founded by a merger of nursing unions in 2009 and, in the past 17 years,has grown considerably from its initial strength of 150,000. The latest victory for NNOC took place in the first week of November when nurses who work for Endeavor Health at Edward Hospital in suburban Naperville, voted by a margin of 65 percent in favor of joining the union. By adding another 1,200 nurses to the Chicagoland area, NNOC now represents over 10,000 members in the region. Nurses at Chicago’s Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital voted 96 percent in favor of unionizing in June of 2026 – days after going on a one-day strike six days before the vote had even occurred- over the unlawful termination of nurses who were advocating for having a collective voice in their workplace. St. Mary Hospital was acquired by Prime Healthcare in March of 2025, and nurses were motivated to take action following drastic changes they experienced in patient care, following cost-cutting measures taken by Prime to boost their bottom line. Nurses at St. Mary struck again for one day on September 3. On September 15, nurses at Olympia Fields Hospital in suburban Chicago, also owned by Prime Healthcare, went on a one-day strike, also voting with an 82 percent margin to join the union about a week afterwards, adding another 400 nurses to NNOC. In early December, 2,400 nurses at four hospitals in the northern Chicago suburbs owned by Endeavor will have an opportunity to vote to organize with Teamsters Union Local 743. Across the United States, there are almost 4.5 million registered nurses, and about one in five of them are in unions – double the overall unionization rate of workers in this country. There are various factors at play behind these statistics, with the most notable ones being a response to chronic understaffing, post-COVID pandemic exhaustion, and the leverage that comes with the relatively higher job security that nurses have. I am a NNOC member, a nurse who works part-time at Cook County’s Stroger hospital, and recently was in conversation with three nurses from St. Mary Hospital and one nurse from RUMC. They had all led successful campaigns to unionize their hospitals with NNOC in the spring of 2026. The testimony of these nurses is useful for understanding what is pushing nurses to organize themselves, the challenges they are confronting in these campaigns, and what the future holds for healthcare workers fighting for justice. Mary, a nurse who works at RUMC, reported on how her coworkers joined the organizing campaign at St. Mary, on the heels of the RUMC vote to join NNOC. She said, “The most inspiring thing was seeing nurses come together for St. Mary’s. It came at the perfect time for us because everyone was so hyped up and excited and ready to jump into action. Seeing people [at RUMC] commit the time, not just for ourselves, but for other nurses in the community to make all nurses in Chicago, and the country, to make work better for them – was really inspiring.” Working conditions were a major driver of nurse unionization. Richard, a nurse at St. Mary, described what motivated him to organize after Prime took over. “Things just got worse and worse. One of the things that happened is my coworker got his ribs broken and he got a black eye from being beaten really badly by a patient because we weren’t staffed properly. I just wanted to be able to have them give us a proper amount of staff under whatever circumstances we have, rather than just applying to some basic rule of one staff to six patients.” Patient safety was a big concern for Jesús, also a nurse at St. Mary, as the employer didn’t want to have “sitters,” someone to watch patients to prevent falls. His unit has “a lot of geriatric dementia patients, and Prime wanted them to be without a sitter, and they were pushing us to admit these patients without one. You can’t really say that patients need a sitter right away, but you’ve seen enough falls and enough adverse complications from falls to know who needs one. They wouldn’t listen to us because the care that patients need, they’re not going to get it, because Prime is trying to squeeze as much juice out of a lemon.” When Mary from RUSH worked as an agency nurse at a unionized hospital, it gave her a glimpse into what conditions might be like. “Nurses wanted to stay and make the hospital a better place to work as opposed to, ‘I’m going to quit and go wherever I feel respected,’ because they do feel respected and appreciated there. Their compensation was on par with other hospitals in the area, and the culture was just more collaborative. Keeping experienced nurses at the bedside was only going to do good things for patients.” Prime Healthcare is a privately held for-profit system, which generates billions of dollars in revenue from its systems across the country, and its assets have only increased since acquiring six more hospitals in the Chicago area. Jesús, who was fired by Prime for advocating for unionization, is directly experiencing their wrath and the wealth they have at their disposal to resist the union. “They have that money. It’s nothing to them because they make billions of dollars off the backs of the patients as well as us.” He continued by saying, “They’re just like, ‘you don’t need any hallway monitors,’ because it just saves them money. They just think, ‘you can take these two patients,’ and they don’t have to pay two nurses. They don’t think about the safety and the potential complications of adverse effects.” Brenda, a nurse at St. Mary, described what provoked nurses to take action. “We decided to go on strike because Prime kept retaliating against our colleagues. They had said that they were going to stop. The day that we received the news of an election date, Prime called two more nurses and left a voicemail that they were terminated because they were, according to Prime, ‘trespassing.’ This was completely false because that’s when we were leafleting, and we had a federal law protecting the right to do that. That’s what made us say, ‘you know what? This is enough.” Richard added, “Our strike was before we had a union, which is unheard of. When our coworkers got fired, a lot of people became very angry. Someone asked me: what was the secret of how you unionized? What was the secret to getting support? The secret to getting support was our company and their war on nurses. A lot of the people became very upset. We won by 96 percent because the company made a lot of nurses very angry.” Even at a so-called non-profit hospital like RUMC, whose policies and practices are nowhere near as nakedly offensive as Prime’s, nurses still overwhelmingly supported unionization. Mary describes how her coworkers saw organizing a union as “having power, having a seat at the table. Having a say in what’s happening to us, what’s happening to our patients. Having a say in our compensation, in our benefits, in our healthcare, in our tuition reimbursement, because that could change whenever Rush wants it. Those benefits could go away at any minute, the only way we can actually secure those is in a contract.” The underlying factor of who ultimately controls the workplace surfaced in both for-profit and non-profit systems. During the unionization campaign, RUMC countered that management had open channels of communication with nurses. Mary described what it looked like: “The hospital’s stance was, ‘We have this great shared governance model. Nurses have so much say. Here are some of the things we’ve taken into account. Here are some of the changes we’ve made.” There was a big push for doing Zoom calls to answer questions, but those questions were very filtered, and we lost our opportunity to talk. Then we lost our cameras. People saw how much Rush was restricting open dialogue, and they were like, “okay.” Jesús described organizing for justice at St. Mary in this way. “It’s a very common issue, and it doesn’t matter what you do, if you’re an Amazon worker or you work in a kitchen, you work. There’s always that power struggle between people trying to make money and you trying to do your job. It’s about the working class coming together.” Brenda reported how workers across different units in the hospital joined together. “It was inspiring how we started to connect unit to unit. Before, ICU [intensive care unit] and emergency room, they are different worlds. In the ICU we’re like, ‘ER is just sending all their patients out to us.’ After getting to know everyone, talking to everyone during the meetings, as well as psychiatry, medical-surgical units… it’s like little towns, right? Getting everyone connected and on the same page, that was one of the best things that we saw.” Jesús went on to describe the importance of links between healthcare workers and their community and how unionization will help stabilize care for patients. “St. Mary has been here a long time. I’ve met people who were like, ‘I was born in this hospital,’ and they have no other place to go, they’re part of the community. Some of them don’t have the pleasure of going to Northwestern or Rush, these fancy hospitals. The community deserves great nurses, but we keep losing nurses to Rush, Northwestern, UIC, and all these other places because St Mary’s cannot compete with them.” Brenda, also from St. Mary, added to this. “With the union, I know that we’re going to get support to fix our staffing grids, and hopefully to retain nurses. Nurses don’t want to do bedside anymore because of the working conditions. During COVID, everyone was a hero, right? All the nurses were heroes. Once that attention went away, they started cutting down. A lot of the things changed about two years ago when Prime took over, and healthcare is now for profit instead of to help our communities.” She further asserted that “healthcare should never bring profit for any company, any government, anything like that. It shouldn’t be a means of profit. In the end, unionization affects our community and affects our patients. With the strike and how much support we had from the community, it was because we’ve taken care of them. We’ve taken care of their kids, we’ve taken care of their families, and themselves. The community knows, and that’s why they were so appreciative and supportive of our movement.” Jesús was one of the multiple nurses that Prime Healthcare had fired during the campaign. Despite this, he shared, “I would still do the exact same thing because regardless of everything that happened, you get further together than just by yourself. We have to organize regardless of where you are, and what you do. At the end of the day you have to work together to make your workplace better. You and your coworkers have a voice which is something that the bosses don’t want you to have.” As was mentioned above, while the 20 percent overall unionization rate of nurses is impressive compared to the average workforce, there is still a lot of room to grow a labor movement of healthcare workers. The overall chronic terrible state of healthcare in this country means there is an ongoing potential to organize patients alongside unions to win significant reforms. A number of newly elected politicians won with a promise of winning healthcare for all. When the Democratic Party majority in Congress gets seated in January 2027, accompanying this event will be severe cuts to Medicaid as a result of Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. These changes will slash about 1 trillion dollars from health services over the next 10 years. Resisting austerity and fighting for the healthcare we deserve will take significant struggle and solidarity between workers and patients – hopefully, the recent victories of nurses in Chicago will help set the stage for successful fights. articles.title: Romania: a growing hub of complicity in genocide
articles.author: Vlad Muresan
articles.content: In April 2026, the opening of yet another Israeli weapons factory in Romania was cause for celebration for some. With great fanfare, Elbit Systems – Israel’s largest private arms manufacturer – inaugurated its seventh production facility in the country, in the small town of Chitila, just outside Bucharest. The company whose weapons have helped sustain Israel’s genocide in Palestine, its decades-long occupation, and its military assaults on Iran was welcomed as a symbol of industrial progress. The event was marked by the test flight of a Watchkeeper X drone and was attended by high ranking Elbit officials, including Uri Maman, VP head of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Operations. The chair of the Senate Defense Committee, a former prime minister and defense minister, as well as an adviser to the serving defense minister were also in attendance. The event received extensive coverage across Romania’s major news outlets. Source: Nicoleta Pauliuc/Facebook At the time of the inauguration, the delivery of Romania’s unmanned aerial systems was already approximately ten months overdue. To date, Elbit has yet to deliver any of the contracted drones, with the delay now extending to 16 months. The company has cited force majeure arising from the war to justify this. In previous months, a significant number of similar Elbit drones were downed over Lebanon, Iran and Iraq. Elbit arms Israel’s attacks beyond Palestine. In Lebanon, its munitions were identified in attacks that killed a Reuters journalist and seven relief volunteers . In Syria, its drones conduct surveillance and strikes. In Iran, its armed drones, surveillance and electronic warfare systems supported Israel’s offensive. Through production, procurement and military cooperation, Romania helps sustain an industry that enables Israel’s regional offensives well beyond Gaza and Palestine. Once a socialist state committed to anti-imperialism, Romania has become an important link in the projection of US imperial power across West Asia, serving as both an operating base for US military aircraft and a production and supply hub within Israel’s military-industrial network. A network of complicity Owned by Simultec, one of the three Romanian Elbit Systems subsidiaries, the Chitila factory is the result of a €380 million contract signed by the Romanian state with the company for seven Watchkeeper X unmanned aerial systems. Romanian production of Watchkeeper X drones spans several companies in Elbit’s supply chain: Simultec manufactures composite airframes, A-E Electronics supplies aircraft components, Eurobody Hydraulics produces ground control stations, and Aerostar integrates the drones’ systems. Watchkeeper X presentation in Chitila, Romania. Source: Elbit System In 2024 and 2025, Israel was Romania’s main military export destination. Military equipment and technology worth over €150 million have been shipped from Romania to Israel. Most of these shipments are presumably coming from Elbit’s own Romanian subsidiaries, which are shipping back to Israel military electronics, drone components and mortar systems for integration into weapons platforms. In the first half of 2026, military exports from Romania to Israel amounted to €34 million. Romania authorized €307.24 million in military exports to Israel in 2025 – nearly 99% through global licenses allowing repeated shipments over several years – and a further €53.6 million in the first half of 2026. Romanian military exports to Israel 2025-2026. Source: ANCEX, Romania’s Department for Export Controls, within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This newest expansion is symptomatic of a process that has been taking place all across Central and Eastern Europe. Under the guise of rearmament, Israeli companies are moving into the area securing record contracts and expanding their production facilities across the region, with Romania becoming one of its central pillars. Read more: Amid mass protests in the West, Israel’s military footprint expands in Eastern Europe This process further integrates the region into the imperialist world system that enabled the genocide in Gaza, while reinforcing Israel’s impunity and undermining international law and institutions. European rearmament creates new opportunities for complicity European rearmament is opening new markets for Israeli arms manufacturers, including through programmes presented as strengthening Europe’s industrial autonomy. Romania’s allocation of up to €16.68 billion in EU-backed loans under Security Action for Europe (SAFE) illustrates the scale of the opportunity. In May 2026, Romania’s General Aviation Inspectorate awarded a €43.18 million helicopter simulation contract to Simultec under the country’s SAFE investment plan. Although registered locally, the company belongs to the Israeli group. These connections also extend through European suppliers. A separate €30.7 million Romanian SAFE contract covers Vector drones from Germany’s Quantum Systems, whose published specifications identify Israel’s NextVision as the supplier of their electro-optical sensors. NextVision supplies imaging components to Elbit Systems, including for drones deployed in Gaza. In 2025, Norway’s largest pension fund, KLP, excluded the company over the risk that its products contribute to violations of international humanitarian law. Elbit Systems lightweight quadcopter. Source: Flightglobal.com Romania’s planned €3.337 billion SAFE procurement of Rheinmetall’s Lynx infantry fighting vehicles also has Israeli links. The configuration described in news reports incorporates Spike LR2 anti-tank missiles produced in cooperation with Israel’s Rafael Advance Defense Systems. In July 2025, Romania signed a €2.04 billion framework agreement for Rafael’s SPYDER air defense systems, followed by a first implementing contract worth approximately €600 million in June 2026. More Israeli companies moving in Israeli military and surveillance companies are expanding their presence in Romania beyond Elbit. IMCO has opened a component manufacturing facility in Crevedia, while Skylock is pursuing local counter-drone production and SAFE procurement opportunities with Optoelectronica. ParaZero and Aero Sentinel have demonstrated their technologies at Romanian military events and exercises. These are all companies deeply embedded in the Israeli military and responsible for genocide, apartheid and occupation in Palestine. Read more: In Eastern Europe, resistance grows to militarism and Israeli arms production The network also extends into surveillance: Cognyte operates a growing software development centre in Bucharest, while Romanian prosecutors have launched a procurement procedure for Cellebrite phone-extraction tools, whose use against journalists and activists abroad has raised serious human rights concerns. Some Romanians are resisting Elbit Out! is a campaign started in 2025 against a concrete infrastructure of complicity. It targets the fact that Israeli military companies are present in Romania, that they profit in Romania, that they produce in Romania, and that the Romanian government uses public money to strengthen them. Its internationalist approach connects solidarity with Palestine to opposition to the governments, corporations and military partnerships that sustain destruction across the Global South. It brings together struggles against war and austerity, demanding that public resources serve people’s needs. The Elbit Out! campaign published its second report in November 2026. Source: Elbit Out!/Facebook The campaign challenges the system that makes genocide profitable and turns Eastern Europe into a market, production base and source of debt for Western and Israeli weapons manufacturers. In November 2026, Elbit Out! published its second report , documenting how Romania has deepened its ties with Israel’s military-industrial complex through arms exports, public procurement and local weapons production. Released as the campaign enters its second year, the report exposes the growing gap between Romania’s professed commitment to international law and its continued economic and military cooperation with companies implicated in Israel’s crimes in Palestine and across the region.

articles.title: The end of an era? ANC suffers historic collapse in South Africa
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: South Africa’s Communist Party just broke away at the ballot box: For the first time since the end of apartheid, the SACP ran on its own ticket in municipal elections, winning 271 seats as Nelson Mandela’s ruling ANC party lost its majority on more than 100 councils – its worst-ever election result. Phel Parkies, the SACP’s national head of elections, joins BT Live to break down the historic shift in South African politics. Parkies says the ANC’s showing reflects the party’s “irreversible decline,” having forfeited the peoples’ trust and confidence through collapsing municipal services and the “voracious accumulation” of corrupt local officials. He says the SACP’s result is a victory for the working class; the party’s mission is socialism in South Africa, “not a consolidation of neoliberalism in our land.” Parkies traces the split back to the ANC’s 1996 adoption of the GEAR economic strategy for “Growth, Employment and Redistribution,” which he says cost the country jobs and deepened inequality: “We believe, as the Communist Party, it was a selling out.” And while the SACP hasn’t left the Tripartite Alliance with the ANC and COSATU, Parkies says it’s now focused on building a broader left unity front – the Conference of the Left – to fight austerity and neoliberalism: “there’s no party that can do that alone.” For the SACP, Parkies says, November 4, 2026 was a turning point: “South Africa is not the same, and it will not be the same.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today!

articles.title: The return of the bases: why Filipinos are fighting Pax Silica
articles.author: Atul Chandra
articles.content: On Sunday, as Southeast Asian leaders gathered in Manila for the 49th ASEAN Summit, the Philippine police carried out what activists call the largest single-day crackdown in decades of Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s presidency. At Sucat People’s Park in Muntinlupa, a designated freedom park, police took more than 300 people into custody. Eight more were seized at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila as they tried to march towards the summit venue. Television footage showed police brutally arresting and detaining them. The National Union of Journalists of the Philippines (NUJP) says at least 22 media workers were harassed who were covering the protests. Who were they ? Farmers, students, indigenous people and workers. What united them was a demand that the guest of honor of the ASEAN Conference would rather not hear: Scrap Pax Silica. President Donald Trump lands in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. It is his first visit since 2017, and nearly 20,000 police officers have been deployed across the capital to receive him and other ASEAN leaders. He is expected to pressure Southeast Asian governments to join Pax Silica. To understand why so many Filipinos are willing to be arrested to stop it, we must go back to 1991. That year, the Philippine Senate did something few small nations dare to do. It voted to end the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Security that allowed the United States to keep military bases on Philippine soil. That same year, Mount Pinatubo erupted and buried Clark Air Base under ash. By the end of 1992, the last American warships had sailed out of Subic Bay. For a generation, Filipinos told this story with pride. The bases were gone. Thirty-five years later, the Americans are returning to Clark. This time they are bringing data centers. Pax Silica’s first physical project is approximately around 4000 acres AI industrial hub at Luzon Economic Corridor, on part of the old Clark air base. Under pressure from the streets, the US ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton, now says no announcement will be made at the summit, and Manila hopes to sign before the year ends. The deal has been delayed. Sunday’s arrests show how far the government will go to keep it alive. A peace written in Washington The US State Department launched Pax Silica in December 2025. It brings together the countries that matter in the “silicon stack”: the mines, power plants, chip factories, computing centers and AI models on which the digital economy runs. About two dozen governments have signed, from Japan and South Korea to India, Israel, and Kazakhstan. The name is no accident. The Pax Romana was the long “Roman peace” that began in 27 BCE, imposed on the Mediterranean world by Rome’s legions and paid for by tribute from conquered provinces. The Pax Britannica was the century after 1815, when the Royal Navy ruled the seas and Britain’s empire stretched from India to Africa. The Pax Americana is the order the United States built after 1945, resting on the dollar and on hundreds of military bases around the world. Those at the center called each of them peace. For those at the edges, they meant conquest, plunder and wars fought far from the imperial capital. Pax Silica openly claims a place in this line. The man who drew up this one is Jacob Helberg, the State Department’s Undersecretary for Economic Affairs. Before taking office, he was a senior adviser to the chief executive of Palantir, the company that builds surveillance and targeting software for armies and spy agencies. Pax Silica was born where Silicon Valley meets the security state. The official story is that Pax Silica protects supply chains from China as evident with the term “coercive dependencies.” This argument gained more strength with the Reuters report revealing a draft State Department letter to 35 countries warning them against “duplicative initiatives whose expectations conflict with our own.” The terms of loyalty are strict. The immediate target is China’s new World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO). But the message reaches every partner. Your choices are no longer entirely your own. This is the old politics of the client state, rewritten for the age of AI. That is part of the truth, but only part. Its deeper purpose is to decide who controls the technologies of the coming century, and on whose terms. Inside the bloc, the roles are already fixed. Washington and its tech giants keep the most advanced AI models, write the standards and hold the off switch. Partners provide the land, the water, the minerals and the labor. Critics warn this creates a trap of “ trusted interdependence .” The bases come back Return now to Clark and look at the map around it. The Port of Subic Bay, once one of the largest US naval bases overseas, has been named the official maritime gateway for Pax Silica. Further north lie the military sites that US forces use under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement . There are now nine of them. A US Typhon mid-range missile system has been stationed on Luzon since April 2024, and during this year’s Balikatan war games US anti-ship missile launchers were set up at one of these sites. Philippine officials insist that the AI hub is purely commercial . But commerce and war are hard to separate when the goods are chips and critical minerals. Rare earths guide missiles. Semiconductors fly drones and run radars. Manila’s new rules on critical minerals could open about nine million hectares to mining exploration. This is why the people’s alliance BAYAN calls Pax Silica war production disguised as development. China is the obvious rival in this design, and Washington makes no secret of it. Yet the logic of empire runs wider than any single rival. The United States wants Asia’s land, labor, minerals and loyalty organized around its own arms industry and tech monopolies, whoever the enemy of the day may be. The membership list reflects that. Israel, a founding signatory, has used AI targeting systems in its war on Gaza. Kazakhstan holds vast mineral wealth on China’s western border. Singapore guards the Strait of Malacca. These are not simply markets. They are chokepoints, mines and frontlines. Who pays the price The price is being paid first in Tarlac. As reported, in the village of Sapang Kawayan, about 200 Aeta families have received letters from the state developer telling them they must relocate. The Aeta are the Indigenous people of the Pinatubo foothills, and many were driven from their homes once before by the eruption of 1991. “They should just have us killed because we will fight for our land,” said Casamira Capiz Maniego, who is 72. The Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) insists that only 40 households are affected and that no one “will be displaced.” The land is only the beginning. According to Mongabay , the hub would need about 3 gigawatts of electricity and between 60 and 90 million liters of water every day. Filipinos already pay the highest household electricity rates in Southeast Asia. Farmers nearby fear for their water in the dry season, and environmental groups say the authorities have produced no hydrological studies . Opposition now reaches far beyond the left. Caritas Philippines, the social action arm of the Catholic Church, opposes the hub in its present form. Bishop Gerardo Alminaza says the project is being rushed, with too little consultation with the Aeta. The mayor of Capas, the town that would host the hub, says local officials were never consulted. In September, police arrested five paralegals and detained nearly 30 people outside a hotel hosting a Pax Silica forum. Sunday’s mass arrests are the same pattern on a larger scale. An empire that needs cheap land and quiet communities abroad also needs governments willing to silence their own people. While the land, the water and the labor come from the South, the profits, the patents and the power stay in the North. None of this means the Global South should turn its back on technology. Developing countries need chips and AI. But they need them on their own terms, through technology transfer, public investment and cooperation among themselves, and with the consent of the communities whose land and water are at stake. Pax Silica offers none of this. Southeast Asia knows that refusal is possible. Of the eleven ASEAN members, only Singapore and the Philippines have joined . In 1991, Filipinos showed the world that foreign bases could be sent home. The farmers, students and Aeta who filled the jails of Metro Manila on Sunday are carrying that memory forward. They are not against technology. They are against being made the raw material of someone else’s empire. Atul Chandra is the Asia co-coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research . articles.title: ‘The city knew’: Who’s to blame for the deadly Brooklyn collapse?
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: “The city knew.” The Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people, including two children, wasn’t a freak accident, says Jaylen Strong, a New York City organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation. It was the predictable result of a housing system where landlords profit from neglect, and where Black, Brown and immigrant tenants pay the price. Joining BT Live’s Zoe Alexandra, Strong points out that a building with nearly 100 open city violations would never have been left to crumble in a wealthier neighborhood. He links the collapse at 1321 Flatbush Avenue to Trump’s ICE raids that keep families hiding at home, and to a government that has money for war on Iran but not for public housing. Seeing the rubble at Flatbush and Bedford, he says, “you can’t help but think of Palestine.” From West Africa to Central America, Strong says, people look at Flatbush and recognize their own struggles. The building’s Olufemi Falade had made the city’s Worst Landlord Watchlist six times, and the construction site next door – a Robert Fischman development built by Townhouse Builders – had already been cited for unsafe excavation. Now, Strong says, the fight is to make sure those responsible for this tragedy are held to account, and that displaced families get permanent homes – not temporary hotel rooms where, he says, there’ve been reports of mice. Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: [Speaker 1:] A building collapse could happen at any moment. We’ve seen this happen. For landlords who operate in poor, working Black immigrant communities, this kind of neglect is profitable. Even if it doesn’t end in a tragedy like this, people make money off of this neglect and a system that’s deliberately built on racial exclusion, ignoring the possibility of danger to the most expendable communities. [Speaker 2:] Last Wednesday afternoon, a three-story mixed-use building on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn collapsed into a construction pit next door. Eight people were killed, two of them children. Nearly 20 more were injured. The building housed working families and apartments above a street-level storefront. Families who lived there lost everything. Their homes were suddenly cut open to the street, closets and bedrooms exposed, hanging open in the rubble for the whole city to see. The warning signs were there. The building had nearly 100 open violations with the city, including citations for exposed wiring and missing smoke detectors. Its landlord had made the public advocate’s worst landlord watch list six times. Next door, the construction site where crews were digging for a planned nine-story building by developer Robert Fishman with Townhouse Builders as a general contractor had already been cited for unsafe excavation and demolition. Brooklyn’s district attorney has opened a criminal investigation, but residents and organizers say they’ve heard promises of accountability before with little follow-through. Joining us now is Jaylen Strong, a Brooklyn-based organizer with the Party for Socialism and Liberation. Jaylen, thanks so much for joining us here. [Speaker 3:] Thank you, Zoe. Thanks for having me on. I’m glad to be back. [Speaker 2:] It’s really hard to call it anything but a tragedy, what happened in Flatbush last week. Unfortunately, it is not necessarily a new phenomenon for New York City. Talk to us about this cycle of landlord neglect and tenants paying the price. [Speaker 3:] You’re right. What happened on November 11th in Flatbush, where this complete tragedy occurred, is not new at all. It’s a stalwart of New York City history and system. It’s not an isolated event. This long-documented history of building failures, construction negligence, aging infrastructure, and chronic disinvestment in the most exploited communities, the most working-class Black and Brown communities, is a long-term part of New York history. The Bedford Avenue building collapse sits not only in this history but also in a cluster of recent structural emergencies and catastrophes that are completely preventable. This tragedy is something many people haven’t seen in a long time to this degree, especially because it’s so deadly. We lost the lives of eight innocent people, two of them children. It’s impossible to think this could have happened in our neighborhood, in our city, in the richest country in the world, where democracy and rights are touted as abundant. But that’s clearly not true from what we see. When you look at the video, you see firefighters excavating and digging in a rescue mission for people who, in the middle of their lives, fell into a pit. It’s a horrible metaphor for how the system works, how capitalism works, and how deadly it is when you look at these videos of rubble and destruction and the insides of people’s homes and lives. This culpability is part of a long history in New York City, but more so about the capitalist system in the United States. The landlord system, the system of greed, negligence, and what is possible when people see life as expendable and put profit over people. It’s a complete shame that this could happen, especially in a neighborhood where I have family, where I have little children coming into the world, cousins, babies. This is something that could have happened to our families, and it’s something that I see as a community, as something very close to my heart, such a tragedy that is completely avoidable. [Speaker 2:] Truly heartbreaking. Before we dig into the element of landlord greed, I wanted to bring up another element that’s come out in a lot of the reporting, which is that several of the victims of this collapse were undocumented immigrants. I read one report that one family had been trying to stay at home, where it seemed like a safe place, because of the presence of ICE and the constant threat of detention and deportation. Talk to us about that element, that many of the people living in this building were either from an immigrant community or undocumented themselves. How does that play into this tragedy? [Speaker 3:] Absolutely. Outside of the obvious structural issues, the fact that people would have to hide in their homes because they are immigrants or migrants to this country is completely absurd. Hiding from ICE on a daily basis is something we’re hearing about in every immigrant community in New York City and almost across the country. People are afraid to go outside and go about their lives. That’s an insane reality constructed by the Trump administration at large, but also the existence of ICE as it stands. It’s an agency that has been let off the leash in every major city in this country. It’s absurd that someone would be completely retreated from reality, retreated from daily life, and afraid to go out on the street. The force of ICE, the violence, the murders we’ve seen across the country, people in a state of fear and shock, is absurd. This is not a reality we will accept. It adds to the layering aspects that not only was the structural issue of the building collapsing the core element relating to the capitalist class, but it also relates to this large struggle and fight against ICE, which is happening in every major city. It’s confounding to think that both of these things could happen at once, but it’s the reality we are seeing and observing and that we refuse to let happen. We have to fight back against it. It becomes a twofold issue that relates to the same enemy and the same root cause. [Speaker 2:] Let’s dig in about this landlord and how the city has responded. This building had nearly 100 open violations. The landlord was on the worst landlord watch list six times. The site next door had already been cited for unsafe excavation. Everyone seems to have known this was a ticking time bomb. Why do you think the warnings didn’t stop this? Who bears responsibility for that failure? [Speaker 3:] The city knew. That’s what those documents show, that the city knew. This pattern is not one of a rare accident. It’s part of systemic neglect, and that systemic neglect falls hardest on communities from which political power is most stolen. The responsibility is shared among the developer, the landlord, and the city enforcement apparatus that repeatedly failed to do anything about these documented hazards. This is a pattern that happens all the time. A building collapse could happen at any moment. For landlords who operate in poor working Black immigrant communities, this kind of neglect is also profitable. Even if it doesn’t end in a tragedy like this, people make money off of this neglect and a system deliberately built on racial exclusion, ignoring the possibility of danger to the most expendable communities. If a building had violations like this in one of the wealthier neighborhoods in New York City or New York State, you would see a different outcome. The way housing functions in this city, the racial wealth gap persists today under the system of housing in the United States. The responsibility is with the builders, the landlords, the owners, the contractors at the demolition site, the special investigators and inspectors who are supposed to make sure things like this don’t happen, the firms, the engineers. There are countless people to blame. But at its core, we’re talking about the system that would allow for it to happen, a system that allows for tragedies like this to become a constant phenomenon. This constant cycle of neglect and the people who pay the price are tenants, working people. It’s unfathomable to think about. This responsibility is the system’s to bear truly. [Speaker 2:] In this moment, there are mass strikes in Spain demanding dignified housing against the housing crisis. We’re seeing cases like this happening in other cities in the United States as well. Perhaps not a building collapse as such, but this constant demand for dignified and safe housing, skyrocketing rent prices, even in cities that used to be cheaper. Do you see this as something isolated to New York City? How do you understand it within a nationwide context? [Speaker 3:] I see it as an issue of austerity, the rising cost of living, and it’s all related to the choices of the government and the system. There’s more money for war, but not for housing, public housing, or socialized housing. There isn’t money for affordable food, but there’s money to go to war with Iran for no exact reason except for the will of the president and the functionaries of the White House. This is a national issue affecting everyday affordability crises, but it also becomes an international issue. When you look at the photos of the building, you can’t help but think of Palestine, Gaza, to see rubble and the openings of people’s homes in destruction. Your mind and heart go to what we’ve seen in the genocide in Palestine. This kind of destruction makes you think of what has happened across the globe under US imperialism for decades. It becomes a national issue because almost everybody working experiences the crisis we are going through right now when it comes to living dignified lives, having permanent housing, being with our families, friends, and living the lives we deserve. There’s a deep interconnectedness between what we see happening here in the United States and everywhere across the world. Deterioration happens to the most exploited. We are an exploited class here, working people, but also all across the world under the boot of imperialism. It becomes an issue relatable not just to the everyday American but to anyone forced to live in squalor despite their efforts to remove themselves from precarity and build the lives they want. People in West Africa, Korea, Central America, and elsewhere have been watching this story closely because this kind of tragedy happening in the United States is a clear sign of what is happening in the country today and abroad. At a rally outside the collapsed building, an organizer shared that a person from Palestine donated to help the families impacted, providing supplies. This person, under the boot of imperialism, occupation by the Israelis, saw what was happening in New York City and Flatbush and felt a responsibility to help. It truly is a large issue, a national issue, but I see it as a much broader instance that calls for solidarity, organizing, and work against the system of housing in the United States that’s been profit-first for decades. Housing should be free for all. [Speaker 2:] Finally, Jaylen, what does a demand for justice look like for the victims and their families of the collapsed building at Bedford? [Speaker 3:] Right now, families from the city are staying in hotels. There have been reports that these hotels are not up to standard, with mice in the hotel. Putting people in situations where their lives are again not respected. This first response by the city’s bureaucracy is not enough. The real demand for justice is permanent and affordable housing. The real demand for justice is the abolition of ICE. The real demand for justice is moving away from a system that allows people to be afraid in their homes and also be in the precarity of maybe not even having a home. There needs to be permanent and affordable housing. There needs to be the prosecution of those culpable, the landlord, the developer. This needs to happen. This is the real crime. The system treats need as crime, but this is the true crime, where innocents have lost their lives. The demands are that this needs to be investigated, prosecuted, and those affected need permanent and affordable housing. But everyone in this country deserves that. This should not be a question in 2026 that people don’t have places to sleep, that in the richest city, in the richest country in the world, people are sleeping on the street, houseless, cold. It’s unfathomable that this is the reality. We have to continue to fight and build and activate our communities to have political agency in this fight, a fight we will win, but one right now seeing complete catastrophe and it will galvanize millions of people. [Speaker 2:] Very powerful. Jaylen Strong from Brooklyn, thank you so much for joining us here at BT Live and for all of your work in this heartbreaking moment in our city, but there is an important path forward. [Speaker 3:] Thank you so much, Zoe.

articles.title: Voices from Turkey: “The More Oppressive the Regime Gets, the More Resilient People Become”
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We are broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. As climate negotiations enter their crucial final days, dozens of human rights groups have urged Turkish authorities to release four LGBTQ activists ahead of a hearing that’s just begun at a court in Istanbul. They’re among dozens of human rights defenders who’ve been imprisoned or subjected to criminal investigations and a large-scale crackdown on LGBTQ groups that began in September. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Turkish authorities also raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sözcü TV and took the channel off the air, while appointing a trustee to run the channel and its website. Four executives from that TV network have also been detained. Since last month, the two remaining opposition channels have been brought under government control. This follows the Turkish government’s widespread crackdown on the main opposition party, with dozens of mayors arrested since 2024. Despite the growing repression, here in Antalya, many of the Turkish groups critical of the government marched alongside international civil society groups this weekend to mark the Global Day of Action. They are also gathered in large numbers at the People’s Climate Summit, an alternative gathering organized by a coalition of Turkish environmental groups that’s taking place in another part of Antalya. We stopped by on Sunday, and I spoke to organizers of the People’s Climate Summit. This is Zişan Tokaç, an activist from Istanbul. ZIŞAN TOKAÇ: My name is Zişan. I am an organizer with the People’s Climate Summit. There are a lot of participants, from government agencies, from corporations, as well, under different badges, as well as from social movements around the world, and they are all in conference halls discussing the future of the climate. And we are here to say that there are people who are excluded from these conference halls. There are people who don’t have the right badges to enter those conference halls, and our voices are not heard in these conference halls. However, these people are also the exact people who are going to be impacted the most by climate change, or who are actively being impacted the most by climate change. So, what People’s Climate Summit does is to bring the people’s voices into the light of the media, the participants of COP31, and raise our demands, because our demands are very different from what governments and corporations want to agree on at these summits. AMY GOODMAN : That was Zişan Tokaç, an activist from Istanbul. We also spoke to Ecehan Balta from the Climate Justice Coalition. She’s based in Ankara and one of the many Turkish activists who’ve been denied entry into the COP this year. She’s a longtime academic and activist who’s worked with rural communities across Turkey fighting for their lands. I began by asking her if she could enter the U.N. climate summit, where we are. ECEHAN BALTA : Actually, I tried to get one. Actually, I got one for the green zone. Then they canceled without no reason. So — AMY GOODMAN : Who is they? ECEHAN BALTA : The Turkish government canceled my entrance to the green zone. So, we cannot be there. I mean, there are some friends and comrades inside trying to reach their voices to their leaders, to the leaders, but we are not one of them. I’m not one of them. AMY GOODMAN : Last year, we were in Belém, in Brazil. We were in the gateway to the Amazon. ECEHAN BALTA : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : Place us, for us, geographically and the kind of climate challenges you face here in Turkey. ECEHAN BALTA : This year in Turkey is in some different contexts. Especially it’s important that it’s — the summit is being held on the border of — on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, which is the almost hottest seas in the world, and it’s getting hot day by day because of the — and they are building a nuclear power plant very close to here, in Mersin, and that will also, you know, contribute the heat of the Mediterranean Sea. AMY GOODMAN : When people organize in Turkey around environmental issues, how does the government respond? ECEHAN BALTA : Actually, the response changes from the region to region. But in general, they attack people. And we generally try to use the processes of laws, and we try to get, you know, positive decisions from the courts. But they never apply, and they are decided by the companies. And they force people to get out from the mining areas, for example. It was the case in Akbelen. They are planning to take the people out from 43 villages, in order to expand the mining area. And we have the court cases. We have the positive decisions. But the government itself doesn’t apply them, and they force people with the — I mean, by the military force to get out from those regions. This is the general case in Turkey. AMY GOODMAN : Ecehan Balta from the Climate Justice Coalition, speaking to us at the People’s Climate Summit over the weekend, about 20 minutes from where we are at the U.N. climate summit. I also spoke to Ömer Madra, one of Turkey’s best-known voices on climate change. He’s a longtime climate activist and beloved broadcaster here in Turkey, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of what was for 29 years Turkey’s only independent community radio station, Açık Radyo, which means Open Radio. In November of 2024, Turkey’s High Commission of Television and Radio revoked Açık Radyo’s FM license after a guest on one of the shows used the phrase “Armenian genocide.” Turkish authorities initially imposed a five-day broadcast ban on the show, later pulled their FM license completely, based on claims that the station had failed to comply with the initial suspension. Forty days later, Açık Radyo, or Open Radio, was reborn as an online radio station called Apaçık Radyo, or Wide Open Radio. It had to open as a different name. I began by asking Ömer Madra why he started Open Radio, Açık Radyo, back in 1995. ÖMER MADRA : I mean, Açık Radyo, since its inception, has been actively engaged in the struggle against all these kinds of anti-democratic things. I mean, you know, my first street protest was in 1965, and now I’m on my 61st year of protesting in the streets. I’m a street boy, as you might — AMY GOODMAN : You’re now how old? Eighty-one? ÖMER MADRA : Eighty-one. More. Well, 81-and-a-half. I have always felt myself a member of the ’68 rebellion generation or revolutionary generation. AMY GOODMAN : And, in fact, Juan González was a part of that ’68 revolutionary change. I mean, he was one of the leaders of the Columbia student strike. He went on to co-found the New York chapter of the Young Lords, the Puerto Rican equivalent of the Black Panthers, and one of the great journalists of the United States. ÖMER MADRA : I’ve been following you with very much admiration, and very strictly, I should say. AMY GOODMAN : For a global audience, what should we understand about Turkey? ÖMER MADRA : Oh, it’s rather difficult. I mean, it has been under the real stress of authoritarianism, getting worse and worse all the time. This started as a democracy, you know, president at the time a former politician, Erdoğan. And he was a reformist in his — in his first three or four years, and maybe more than that. That’s why I believe he was reelected with his party. But then, in what we see in many other European countries, as well, and in very many parts of the world, in many countries, there has been a trend towards, if not fascism, but anti-democratic, and the government of Turkey also chose that path. And we have — I do believe that we have none other thing to do than to resist such thing and struggle for a full democracy all the time. AMY GOODMAN : So, you have a team coming to Antalya to cover the climate summit, COP31. You’re inside, and you’re outside the COP . How would you frame the climate issue, in Turkey and globally? ÖMER MADRA : The biggest problem is global climate change, of course, or global warming. But the second very big problem is that there is no free media to talk about this. Almost 90% of the Turkish people were not aware of COP or COP31. AMY GOODMAN : Apaçık Radyo, what it’s called now, very Wide Open Radio, is the same age as Democracy Now! It’s 30 years old. It’s more than — ÖMER MADRA : We’re a bit older. AMY GOODMAN : Oh, really? ÖMER MADRA : One — one year older. AMY GOODMAN : You think you’re more mature? ÖMER MADRA : Not mature, but our birthday is a bit — one year older. AMY GOODMAN : And I want to thank you for running Democracy Now! on your radio station, ÖMER MADRA : Amy, thank you so much. I mean, it’s my great pleasure. AMY GOODMAN : That’s Ömer Madra, the co-founder and editor-in-chief of Apaçık Radyo, or Wide Open Radio. It used to be called Open Radio, or Açık Radyo, until it was taken off the airwaves two years ago, is now available online. For more on the state of repression and dissent here in Turkey, we’re joined now by Berkan Özyer, the director of Greenpeace Türkiye. Thanks so much for being with us. Usually, you deal with environmental issues, but I want you to talk about this level of pressure. I mean, even in the midst of the U.N. climate summit, two Turkish opposition stations are taken over by the Turkish government. And in the lead-up to it, if you can explain what’s happened to many dissenters, and especially the LGBTQ community? BERKAN ÖZYER: Welcome. Thank you. First, it depends on how you look at the things. From the eyes of a person who actually lives here, and this — this trend goes on for years. And also, if you look at the bigger picture, it’s also another global trend starting to get accelerated also. So, as Turkey, we are one of the, let’s say, pioneers of this unfortunate global trend. So, but the main thing is, because of the lack of leader in the leadership, there’s a power vacuum within this system in terms of values, so there is no one to judge. Even when you are hosting hundreds-plus world leaders in your own city, in your own country, you can also still do this, because there is no one to, you know, judge you or make you pay a price. But on the contrary, there is another point we need to focus. Just like to People’s Summit — you were there — this also, the more oppressive regime gets, the more resilient people become. This is the most important part for us, as well, because as we saw in the streets of Antalya, as we have been seeing in the streets of many different cities of Turkey, there is a popular demand for a change. Whether it should be about environment, whether it should be about women issues or LGBTQ movements, there is a demand for change. And it will be happening. And we want to make it real when it happens. AMY GOODMAN : And, I mean, there was a mass protest on Saturday, thousands of people, but it was international. And it seemed like the Turkish dissidents within the protesters felt safer, even with the rainbow flag, waving it, because they felt protected by this international mass protest. BERKAN ÖZYER: Exactly. This is like the old saying: “Together, we stand.” You know, it goes for the same country, as well, but on the global stage also. The system, especially focused on securitization, wants to feel us alone, you know, insecure. But when you come together with your comrades, your friends from all around the world, from all around the city, as we saw just couple of days ago here in the streets of Antalya, you see that we are not alone in these fights, in the struggle against changing the system. This was a great example for us, as well. AMY GOODMAN : And last question on the environment. You are the head of Greenpeace Türkiye. Explain coal phaseout, why also Turkey has become the largest importer of plastic waste from the EU, from the European Union. BERKAN ÖZYER: Two things: lack of monitors, lack of audits, and lack of system. This is the biggest thing. Coal is very, how to say, bad for the environment, air pollution, human health issues, soil, water. It is bad for environment, and especially for economic reasons, as well. If you have a socioeconomic crisis like we do in Turkey, the price becomes even more higher. So, there has to be a coal phaseout announced immediately. This is the first thing we are asking. And second, we’ve become the biggest plastic waste importer from the EU and the U.K., as Turkey, because it was China up until 2018, and they put a ban on it, and then Turkey replaced due to logistic reasons. And it’s a dirty business. There is a lot of informalities around this. There is a lot of human rights abuse about this. So, this has to be — and also, you know, it gives you, gives your image — it expresses your stance in your position about the global trade. So, we don’t want to be none of — we don’t want any other country to export plastic waste of other countries. This is against — a fight against the whole plastic industry itself. The root cause is the plastic industry, and we are against it. AMY GOODMAN : Berkan Özyer, I want to thank you so much for being with us, director of Greenpeace here in Turkey. Coming up, Colombia’s former environment minister. She chaired the landmark Santa Marta Conference earlier this year on transitioning away from fossil fuels. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Music performed at last week’s World Leaders’ Summit for COP31. Page 2 This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit — that’s COP31, conference of parties, 31 years — here in Antalya, Turkey. Over 90,000 people have participated in this summit over the last week and a half. It’s considered the largest. Negotiators have just a few more days to see if they can come to some final agreement. Despite all the many significant issues being debated here, from climate finance to electrification, what’s not discussed is also significant, and that’s the transition away from fossil fuels, the number one driver of global warming. Well, seven months ago, a bloc of nations led by Colombia held a separate conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, with the explicit shared agenda to begin the transition away from fossil fuels. More than 50 countries participated. A group of countries have already released national roadmaps to do just that. Colombia is a significant fossil fuel producer. The country is Latin America’s largest coal exporter, as well as a significant exporter of crude oil. Despite the importance of the fossil fuel industry for Colombia’s economy, the Santa Marta Conference was championed by then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro, whose term ended in August. Colombia’s new right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella has since withdrawn Colombia from the Santa Marta coalition. But the larger process continues. We’re joined now by Irene Vélez-Torres. As Colombia’s acting minister of environment and sustainable development under Petro, she served as co-chair for the Santa Monica Conference along with the Netherlands. She was also the former director of Colombia’s National Environmental Agency and the former minister of mines and energy. We thank you so much for being with us. Those are a lot of titles that you don’t have right now because of the new government in Colombia. But you’re here to represent the Santa Marta coalition. First, the significance of your new president pulling out of the Santa Marta coalition? And explain what it is. IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : The Santa Marta coalition unites 57 governments, but also civil society, subnational governments, parliamentarians, NGOs, who came together in Santa Marta with a very specific, clear message, which is it is needed and urgent to phase out fossil fuels. And because here in these COPS we have the limitation of consensus, then we needed a different — AMY GOODMAN : Which it really isn’t. Consensus is not actually the rule. It’s just the custom. But to make clear to people around the world, fossil fuels are not mentioned when it comes to final documents at the COP summit, which might shock people. IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is really strange for someone that is not part of this diplomatic world to actually know that 80% of the global emissions are connected to fossil fuels, and however, climate change being discussed in these COPs is not addressed from the production and consumption of fossil fuels. The production side of this problem has always been denied. And why is that? Because there are lobbyists, there are petro lobbyists, people here defending the interest of the corporations, and therefore the discussions cannot make any progress. The agreements cannot even mention the word “fossil fuels.” AMY GOODMAN : So, talk about what’s come out of the Santa Marta coalition. You are releasing a report this week. We just heard, after yesterday’s broadcast of Democracy Now! , that countries like Spain are releasing a roadmap. What does that mean? A roadmap to what? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : One year ago, when we were in Belém in the COP30, we were very frustrated, because we couldn’t address the elimination of fossil fuels as part of the dialogues and as part of the official agenda. So, we decided, led by President Petro, that it was needed to create a parallel but connected space. And we decided to host that particular space, to create that particular space in Santa Marta, Colombia. We managed to gather 57 countries with one agreement in order to get there, that the elimination of fossil fuels was necessary and that we needed to do it in an orderly and urgent way. We invited not only governments, but also civil society and subnational governments. And when we were there, we decided that the transition away from fossil fuels had three calls of action: one, to make roadmaps, which implies to plan; second, that the decarbonization of trade is needed, particularly for oil, coal and gas-producing countries like Colombia; and third, that the financial system has to be revised, because, otherwise, especially countries from the Global South won’t have the investment needed in order to make the diversification of economies that are necessary as part of the just transition. So, we have these three work streams already in progress, and we hope that towards the second conference, that is going to take place in Tuvalu in July 2027, we can show more action-oriented decisions by the governments. AMY GOODMAN : When you say “climate finance,” another buzzword that most people don’t understand — loss and damage is within that — if you can explain what it is, what it means when you have the historically biggest carbon polluters in the world, from the United States to China, and those countries feeling the terrible effects then, though not causing it? What is a fair way to help these countries adapt, but also deal with catastrophes, like Nepal — IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : — with a glacier breaking off and killing thousands of people? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes, 31 COPs have been trying to address the problem of financiating actions that could cope with climate change. What kind of actions? Most of them are focused on adaptation, which means to have the tools at the national level to cope with the changes that the increase in global temperatures are going to generate. It was maybe three COPs ago that we also came with the concept of the Loss and Damage Fund, which will mean that all developed countries, the ones that have polluted the most, will put money in a bag, and every country that will feel damages generated by climate change will be able to address that fund. However, the fund is insufficient, and the mechanisms to address that money are super complicated, bureaucratic, very difficult for countries to actually get to those resources. But there is another, blind coronary that I want to point here, which is that this finance is not meant for the diversification of economies, which means that there is no allocation of money for transitioning from producing gas, oil and coal to producing something different, which means that our economic dependency is not really overcome with the kind of finance that is offered in these COPs. AMY GOODMAN : The Colombian government and the U.S. government have signed two new agreements around critical minerals and nuclear energy. What is the significance of this? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is a terrible news for Colombia and its sovereignty. Basically, what happened there is that the Colombian government resigned to sovereignty. And there are particularities about that agreement that should be clearly stated. One, the Colombian government has made explicit that it’s going to ask permission to the U.S. in order to allocate any mining project, which means that it’s like if we were the son that has to ask for permission in order to act, and not a proper government, not a proper state. The second, all the knowledge generated by Colombia as a sovereign country will have to be shared with the U.S., meaning that we don’t have knowledge sovereignty and that everything that is our resources in the subsoil will be known by the U.S. And the third one is that any investment that the U.S. would like to prioritize will have to be also prioritized by Colombia. AMY GOODMAN : Final comments? We have 20 seconds. What people should know around the world about what you want to see come out of COP31? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Let me also say that this government of Colombia has just reversed the protection of the Amazon. Gustavo Petro already had protected 42% of our territory, declaring it a fossil-free zone. And however, this government came and reversed that historical decision, not only for Colombia, but for all the South American countries that share this biome. This is making a huge risk in terms of water integrity, because the water that is generated by the forest of the Amazon also moves towards Bogotá. So, what we are seeing is really an ecocide taking place in Colombia. AMY GOODMAN : Irene Vélez-Torres, former director of Colombia’s National Environmental Agency, also served as Colombia’s acting minister of the environment under President Gustavo Petro. She co-chaired the Santa Marta Conference earlier this year. Coming up, Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at Union of Concerned Scientists. And then we’ll talk about what’s happening in Ecuador. We’re at the U.N. climate summit. Back in a minute. [break] AMY GOODMAN : For our radio listeners, that music break was recorded at the — for our radio listeners, that musical break was recorded at the “Polluters Must Pay” protest here at COP31 in Antalya this morning. In the video, protesters dressed as giant peanuts. Yes, peanuts. They’re dancing while holding up giant pennies that spell out “Pay Up.” A recurring chant at the protest was “Billions, not peanuts,” “Trillions, not peanuts.” They were protesting the inadequate funding and contributions from rich, polluting countries to the countries that need adaptation and recovery funds the most. Page 3 As Democracy Now! continues broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, we speak with Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, about climate finance — the notion that efforts to mitigate the climate crisis must be funded. “Climate finance is not an abstract thing. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit — that’s COP31, conference of parties, 31 years — here in Antalya, Turkey. Over 90,000 people have participated in this summit over the last week and a half. It’s considered the largest. Negotiators have just a few more days to see if they can come to some final agreement. Despite all the many significant issues being debated here, from climate finance to electrification, what’s not discussed is also significant, and that’s the transition away from fossil fuels, the number one driver of global warming. But to make clear to people around the world, fossil fuels are not mentioned when it comes to final documents at the COP summit, which might shock people. IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is really strange for someone that is not part of this diplomatic world to actually know that 80% of the global emissions are connected to fossil fuels, and however, climate change being discussed in these COPs is not addressed from the production and consumption of fossil fuels. The production side of this problem has always been denied. And why is that? Because there are lobbyists, there are petro lobbyists, people here defending the interest of the corporations, and therefore the discussions cannot make any progress. The agreements cannot even mention the word “fossil fuels.” AMY GOODMAN : So, talk about what’s come out of the Santa Marta coalition. You are releasing a report this week. We just heard, after yesterday’s broadcast of Democracy Now! , that countries like Spain are releasing a roadmap. What does that mean? A roadmap to what? We managed to gather 57 countries with one agreement in order to get there, that the elimination of fossil fuels was necessary and that we needed to do it in an orderly and urgent way. We invited not only governments, but also civil society and subnational governments. And when we were there, we decided that the transition away from fossil fuels had three calls of action: one, to make roadmaps, which implies to plan; second, that the decarbonization of trade is needed, particularly for oil, coal and gas-producing countries like Colombia; and third, that the financial system has to be revised, because, otherwise, especially countries from the Global South won’t have the investment needed in order to make the diversification of economies that are necessary as part of the just transition. So, we have these three work streams already in progress, and we hope that towards the second conference, that is going to take place in Tuvalu in July 2027, we can show more action-oriented decisions by the governments. AMY GOODMAN : When you say “climate finance,” another buzzword that most people don’t understand — loss and damage is within that — if you can explain what it is, what it means when you have the historically biggest carbon polluters in the world, from the United States to China, and those countries feeling the terrible effects then, though not causing it? What is a fair way to help these countries adapt, but also deal with catastrophes, like Nepal — IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : — with a glacier breaking off and killing thousands of people? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : Yes, 31 COPs have been trying to address the problem of financiating actions that could cope with climate change. What kind of actions? Most of them are focused on adaptation, which means to have the tools at the national level to cope with the changes that the increase in global temperatures are going to generate. It was maybe three COPs ago that we also came with the concept of the Loss and Damage Fund, which will mean that all developed countries, the ones that have polluted the most, will put money in a bag, and every country that will feel damages generated by climate change will be able to address that fund. However, the fund is insufficient, and the mechanisms to address that money are super complicated, bureaucratic, very difficult for countries to actually get to those resources. But there is another, blind coronary that I want to point here, which is that this finance is not meant for the diversification of economies, which means that there is no allocation of money for transitioning from producing gas, oil and coal to producing something different, which means that our economic dependency is not really overcome with the kind of finance that is offered in these COPs. AMY GOODMAN : The Colombian government and the U.S. government have signed two new agreements around critical minerals and nuclear energy. What is the significance of this? IRENE VÉLEZ- TORRES : It is a terrible news for Colombia and its sovereignty. Basically, what happened there is that the Colombian government resigned to sovereignty. And there are particularities about that agreement that should be clearly stated. One, the Colombian government has made explicit that it’s going to ask permission to the U.S. in order to allocate any mining project, which means that it’s like if we were the son that has to ask for permission in order to act, and not a proper government, not a proper state.
